Chapter 8: The Trap of Despair and the Practice of Hope.
You know, there are days when the world just feels unbearably heavy. The news is packed with stories of violence, injustice, and suffering, and it honestly seems like nothing will ever change.
In moments like these, despair can sneak up on us. It whispers that all our efforts are pointless, and tries to convince us that hope is just some naïve fantasy.
But hope—at least, the kind described in “Strength to Love”—isn’t about wishing problems away or pretending everything’s fine. It’s actually an active choice. It means deciding to keep moving forward, even when you’re not sure where the road leads. It’s that stubborn belief that, no matter how dark things get, there’s still a chance for light.
Picture this: a mother, exhausted after years of struggle, sits at her kitchen table, staring at a pile of unpaid bills. The weight of disappointment and fear presses in on her shoulders. Just then, her child wanders in, needing help with homework. And, almost without thinking, she finds herself smiling. In that small, everyday moment, she remembers—hope isn’t about ignoring pain. It’s about finding reasons to keep going, even when it’s hard.
Most of us don’t even realize how easily we slip into despair, how fast we assume things will never get better. It’s so tempting to just throw in the towel, to let go of our dreams, or to stop trying altogether. But here’s something to pay attention to: every single act of hope—no matter how tiny—is actually an act of resistance. It pushes back against the forces that want to keep us down.
Think about this story: after a devastating storm, a group of neighbors looked around at the destruction in their community. The damage was overwhelming, and honestly, many people just wanted to give up. But then, one person picked up a broom and started clearing debris. Another brought over some food. Little by little, as they worked side by side, hope started to come back. The progress was slow, and the work was tough, but the simple act of coming together made all the difference.
What that shows is that hope isn’t just a feeling. It’s a practice—it’s something we do, over and over, even on the days when we’d rather not. It’s the decision to show up, to keep loving, and to keep believing that change is possible, even when it feels impossible.
A lot of people fall into the trap of thinking hope is only for the lucky or the strong. But that’s just not true. Hope is for everyone. No matter where you are or what you’re facing, hope is a choice you can make—today, and every day after.
